mappings.note: Asks for the definition of a homogeneous mixture and the distractors are heterogeneous behaviours (uneven distribution, settling) -- LO-6's 'explains why a solution is homogeneous'. No particle-size figure is offered, so not LO-14.

A laser is shone through three tumblers and the answer is what the beam does -- LO-15's 'demonstrates the Tyndall effect and uses it to identify a colloid', applied here to the negative case. The sub-nanometre size appears only in the rationale, not in the question or options, so LO-14 is not cited.

Why the solvent must start below the spot is the setup rule of paper chromatography and turns on capillary rise carrying the components -- LO-11's 'explains the principle of paper chromatography'. Nothing about solvent choice, but LO-11 is the only chromatography outcome.
Three statements, each a homogeneous/heterogeneous call, and one of them is an aerated drink -- an example LO-6 names outright. Classification only; no separation or particle-size reasoning.

Same LO-6 classification family as the previous item, here turning on brass (LO-6's named alloy case) and on oil-and-water being heterogeneous. Oil and water is being classified, not separated, so not C8.2-LO-11.

Names which component is solute and which is solvent -- the first clause of LO-7, with no arithmetic. Shares LO-7 with the concentration numericals because the frame puts identification and calculation in one outcome.

A three-way classification of P, Q and R from observations, which is LO-14's job; the light-path column is the only thing that separates the colloid from the solution, so LO-15 does real work here too. Both cited because either alone leaves one of the three mixtures undecidable.

WEAK FIT. Purely conceptual -- why an ORS must hit an exact concentration -- with no calculation and no solute/solvent naming. LO-7 is the only outcome in this frame that mentions concentration at all, so it is cited as nearest; no outcome covers 'why a prescribed concentration matters'.
Straight m/m calculation, 15 g in 85 g of water, with the 85% and 17.6% distractors punishing use of solvent mass instead of solution mass. LO-7.

POOR FIT, and a gap in the frame. The question asks for mass-by-VOLUME percentage (8 g in 200 mL); LO-7 names only mass-by-mass and volume-by-volume. Cited as nearest because it is the sole concentration outcome, but % m/V has no home in curriculum 82's list.

Asks which property makes the separating funnel work, and the key is immiscibility plus a density difference -- LO-11's 'justifies the choice from the properties of the mixture'. The boiling-point distractor is exactly what would make it LO-10 if correct.
Straight v/v calculation, 5 mL in a 250 mL spray. LO-7, same as the other concentration numericals; the frame offers no finer split than m/m versus v/v, and both live in this one outcome.

Assertion is solid solubility rising with temperature, and the reason is a false particle-spacing claim -- LO-8's 'how solubility changes with temperature'. Not LO-9: no crystals form and nothing cools.
Pure definition of a saturated solution, including the at-a-given-temperature qualifier -- the first clause of LO-8. No curve is read, but LO-8 is the only outcome that defines saturation.

Gas solubility falling as temperature rises, with dissolved oxygen and fizz as consequences. LO-8's temperature-dependence clause is the nearest home, though the outcome is written around solids and solubility curves and never mentions gases -- a mild stretch, recorded here. Not LO-6: aerated drinks appear as a gas-solubility case, not a classification one.
Four m/m concentrations computed and compared to find the matching pair (10% for A and C). LO-7, calculation clause.

What happens on slow cooling of a hot saturated solution, answered as 'separates out and forms regular crystals' -- LO-9's principle plus 'describes a crystal as a regular solid'. The solubility-curve phrase is scaffolding; nothing is read off a curve, so not LO-8.

WEAK FIT. The reason for adding dilute sulfuric acid is a bench detail of the copper sulfate preparation, aimed at purity of the crystals. LO-9 owns crystallisation and is the nearest home, but its text (principle, regular solid, slow cooling) does not reach this procedural step.
Cooling rate versus crystal size and regularity, in assertion-reason form -- LO-9's 'explains why slow cooling yields larger crystals' word for word.

Vapour going straight back to solid on the funnel wall is deposition, the second term named in LO-12, and the camphor-from-sand setup is its separation clause. Not LO-9: the distractor 'crystallisation from a saturated solution' is the wrong answer precisely because no solution is involved.

Crystallisation beats evaporation to dryness because soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor -- the purity consequence of LO-9's principle. Distinguished from the part-1 three-way comparison item, which also had to place distillation and so carried LO-10 as well.

The answer is the arithmetic difference between two solubility figures read off a table -- LO-8's temperature-dependence clause. Family rule applied throughout this chapter: reading solubility data is LO-8, while crystal form, size or purity is LO-9. Here the crystals are only a unit of measurement for the solubility drop.

Ordering the four steps of a copper sulfate crystallisation. Not LO-16: that outcome is for separating a mixture of more than two components, whereas this is the internal procedure of one technique on one salt, so LO-9's principle governs.

Glass is the odd one out because it is amorphous -- this tests LO-9's 'describes a crystal as a regular solid'. No solution, cooling or separation is involved, which is what keeps it off the other crystallisation items' ground.

States the condition under which simple distillation is the appropriate method -- a boiling-point gap of about 25 degrees for miscible liquids. LO-10's 'states when each is the appropriate method'. The immiscible distractor is the LO-11 case being ruled out.
